newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: China stalls for time over N.Korean defector crisis.
newsitem.headline: China stalls for time over N.Korean defector crisis.

text.p: China called on Friday for more time to resolve a crisis over North Korea's top communist party theoretician, stranded in a South Korean embasssy compound in Beijing where he is seeking asylum.

Talks in Singapore between South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha and Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen failed to break a deadlock over the defector, Hwang Jang-yop, 73, the most senior Pyongyang official ever to flee the North.

In Beijing, however, a South Korean embassy official said negotiations had begun over Hwang, who spent a second night in the embassy compound with an aide as Seoul and Pyongyang both made hectic efforts to claim him.
"This incident happened all of a sudden, so we need more time to investigate," Qian told reporters after a 50-minute meeting with Yoo in Singapore.
He urged both Koreas "to treat this matter with a cool and calm manner, to keep peace and stability".
Some commentators have suggested Pyongyang, grappling with a food crisis after disastrous floods, might react violently to the defection of a man ranked 24 in its hierarchy.
Yoo told reporters the two sides would meet again, but did not say where or when. He said Friday's talks, scheduled to last 30 minutes, were "good".
The two men met on the fringes of a conference in Singapore of Asian and European foreign ministers.

Hwang is credited with devising Pyongyang's quirky brand of socialism but in letters released in South Korea has now revealed himself as the most prominent critic of a system he says has led to dictatorship and famine.
China has been dragged unwillingly into a heated row that has bred fears of renewed tension on the Korean peninsula and possibly a disastrous collapse of the North.
Chinese police by Friday had moved away several North Koreans watching the compound from cars parked nearby.

"They are harassing us and we are a little nervous about that," said South Korean embassy spokesman Chang Moon Ik, adding that Seoul had asked China to maintain its tight security net around the compound.

One North Korean official, dressed in a suit with a badge of the late North Korean leader Kim Il-sung pinned to a lapel, said he was waiting near the Seoul mission in the hope of persuading Hwang to return home.

"We are waiting here for him to come out and then ask him to come back," said the official, who stood near a Chinese police cordon blocking off the compound and declined to identify himself. "He is our compatriot."
Pyongyang has charged that Hwang must have been kidnapped, and has called on Beijing to sort out the mess.

Seoul has dismissed as "preposterous" Pyongyang's charges that Hwang, one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party, was kidnapped, saying he arrived at the compound in a taxi on Wednesday.

Officials at the North Korean embassy refused to comment or to confirm reports from Seoul that Pyongyang had sent a delegation led by an official at the level of vice-minister and including officials from the ruling Workers Party and the Foreign Ministry to discuss Hwang's defection.
South and North Korea were separated at the end of World War Two and fought a war from 1950 to 1953. China fought on North Korea's side in the conflict.
China is torn between an old socialist comrade and new capitalist friend, but Western diplomats in Beijing believe it has little choice but to respect Hwang's desire to defect.
Tokyo kept its distance, wary of trying to act as honest broker between the Koreas, which both have lingering hatred towards Japan, former colonial overlord of the Korean peninsula.
"We will watch the situation with great interest," top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference. "But will not go any further and get deeply involved."

Hwang defected in Beijing while returning home from a two-week visit to Japan where he lectured on "Juche", a fanatic doctrine of self-reliance that is being cast aside as Pyongyang begs for international food aid.
The stakes are high for Hwang, who holds the innermost secrets of North Korea's government as an intimate of top leader Kim Jong-il, who celebrates his 55th birthday this weekend.

North Koreans caught fleeing can expect summary execution, or a lifetime in the gulag. Families of defectors, according to a fighter pilot who defected last year, are condemned to "a life of slavery".
